stages.name: Contested
stages.desc: Rival fleets fight for these waters

stages.name: Carthaginian
stages.desc: Carthage's fleets and Punic ports hold the coast

stages.name: Syracusan & Greek
stages.desc: Syracuse or other Greek navies hold the coast

stages.name: Roman
stages.desc: Rome's new fleets hold the coast

states.name: Spain
timeline: Phoenician Gades and Punic ports along the south coast trade under Carthage's protection
The second treaty with Rome closes the sea beyond Mastia, near Cartagena, to Roman ships
Spain's silver and mercenaries stay beyond Rome's reach throughout the war

states.name: Libya
timeline: Punic Leptis, Oea and Sabratha hold the Tripolitanian shore; Greek Cyrene lies to the east
Ptolemy of Egypt takes Cyrene; the Altars of the Philaeni still mark the Punic border

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Carthage, the home port of the Punic fleet
Agathocles of Syracuse lands on Cape Bon and burns his ships
Agathocles abandons his army and flees Africa; Carthage holds its coast again
After Ecnomus, a Roman army lands at Aspis and marches on Carthage
Xanthippus defeats Regulus; the Roman fleet evacuates the survivors
Peace: Carthage keeps Africa, but pays 3,200 talents over ten years

states.name: Greece
timeline: Greek city fleets, Athens' above all, hold the Aegean
A Macedonian fleet crushes Athens at Amorgos
Pyrrhus of Epirus sails for Italy to fight Rome

states.name: Italy
timeline: Dionysius of Syracuse destroys Motya; Carthage strikes back across Sicily
Peace leaves Dionysius the strongest navy in the Sicilian and Tyrrhenian seas
Dionysius besieges Lilybaeum; a Punic squadron captures his fleet at Eryx
With Dionysius dead, Punic western Sicily and Sardinia hold firm
Timoleon's victory at the Crimisus revives Syracuse
Carthage defeats Agathocles at the Himera and besieges Syracuse
Agathocles dies and Syracuse's navy declines; Punic ships rule the Tyrrhenian
Pyrrhus of Epirus crosses to Sicily and takes Eryx, but fails at Lilybaeum
The Punic fleet shatters Pyrrhus' ships in the Strait of Messina
Rome crosses to Messana: the First Punic War begins
Duilius' new fleet wins at Mylae, but the Punic navy fights on
Carthage wins at Drepana and storms wreck a Roman fleet
Victory at the Aegates: Rome takes Sicily and the seas around it

states.name: Algeria
timeline: A chain of Punic harbours, such as Hippo and Iol, lines the Numidian coast
Numidian princes waver between Carthage and the invader Agathocles

states.name: Malta
timeline: A Punic island, a harbour on the routes between Carthage and Sicily
A Roman consul raids Malta, but the island stays Punic

events.title: Motya falls
events.text: Dionysius I of Syracuse storms the Phoenician island city of Motya with siege towers and the first catapults.

events.title: Lilybaeum founded
events.text: Survivors of Motya settle on Cape Boeo; the new fortress port of Lilybaeum, today's Marsala, replaces their island.

events.title: Syracuse besieged
events.text: Himilco's army and fleet besiege Syracuse, but plague and a surprise attack destroy them.

events.title: Raid on Pyrgi
events.text: Dionysius' fleet plunders the rich Etruscan sanctuary at Pyrgi, the port of Caere.

events.title: Lilybaeum besieged
events.text: Dionysius besieges Lilybaeum; Carthaginian ships surprise and capture his fleet in the harbour at Eryx.

events.title: Treaty with Rome
events.text: Carthage and Rome renew a treaty that bars Roman ships from Punic waters beyond Mastia in Spain.

events.title: Timoleon sails
events.text: Corinth sends Timoleon with a small fleet to free Syracuse from tyrants and Carthage.

events.title: Battle of the Crimisus
events.text: Timoleon routs a Carthaginian army at the Crimisus river in a thunderstorm.

events.title: Battle of Amorgos
events.text: A Macedonian fleet defeats the Athenian navy, ending Athens' long rule of the Aegean.

events.title: Ptolemy takes Cyrene
events.text: Ptolemy of Egypt seizes the Greek city of Cyrene, Carthage's eastern neighbour.

events.title: Battle of the Himera
events.text: Hamilcar defeats Agathocles of Syracuse at the southern Himera river and besieges Syracuse.

events.title: Agathocles in Africa
events.text: Agathocles slips through the blockade, lands on Cape Bon and burns his own ships.

events.title: Agathocles flees
events.text: Defeated in Africa, Agathocles escapes by sea, leaving his army and sons behind.

events.title: Agathocles dies
events.text: The death of the king of Syracuse leaves Sicily's Greek fleet without a master.

events.title: Pyrrhus in Italy
events.text: King Pyrrhus of Epirus lands in Italy and beats the Romans at Heraclea.

events.title: Punic fleet at Ostia
events.text: Mago brings 120 Carthaginian ships to Ostia to stiffen Rome against Pyrrhus.

events.title: Lilybaeum holds
events.text: Pyrrhus takes Eryx, but Lilybaeum, supplied by sea, withstands his siege.

events.title: Strait of Messina
events.text: As Pyrrhus leaves Sicily, the Carthaginian fleet sinks or captures most of his ships.

events.title: Crossing to Messana
events.text: Rome sends troops across the strait; a Carthaginian decked warship runs aground and is captured.

events.title: Hiero joins Rome
events.text: Hiero II of Syracuse changes sides and becomes Rome's ally and grain supplier.

events.title: Agrigentum falls
events.text: Rome takes Akragas after a seven-month siege and resolves to fight Carthage at sea.

events.title: A fleet from a wreck
events.text: Copying the captured ship, Rome orders 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes, training rowers on benches ashore.

events.title: Lipari Islands
events.text: The consul Scipio and seventeen new ships are trapped and captured at Lipara.

events.title: Battle of Mylae
events.text: Duilius' boarding bridges, the corvus, turn a sea battle into a land fight; Rome wins its first naval victory.

events.title: Battle of Sulci
events.text: Rome beats a Punic fleet off Sardinia; its admiral Hannibal Gisco is crucified by his own men.

events.title: Battle of Tyndaris
events.text: An indecisive clash off northern Sicily; both sides lose ships.

events.title: Malta raided
events.text: The consul Atilius Regulus ravages Malta, a Punic island.

events.title: Battle of Ecnomus
events.text: Some 330 Roman and 350 Carthaginian ships clash off Sicily, one of the largest sea battles ever fought.

events.title: Landing at Aspis
events.text: Regulus lands in Africa and seizes Aspis, modern Kelibia.

events.title: Battle of the Bagradas
events.text: Xanthippus the Spartan, with elephants and cavalry, destroys Regulus' army near Tunis.

events.title: Storm off Camarina
events.text: Returning from Africa, the Roman fleet is caught by a storm; of 364 ships only 80 survive.

events.title: Panormus falls
events.text: A rebuilt Roman fleet of 220 ships helps take Panormus, today's Palermo.

events.title: Siege of Lilybaeum
events.text: Rome blockades Lilybaeum by land and sea; the siege will last nine years.

events.title: The Rhodian
events.text: Hannibal the Rhodian runs the blockade in a fast ship until he is caught; Rome copies his ship.

events.title: Battle of Drepana
events.text: Adherbal traps Claudius Pulcher's fleet against the shore and takes 93 Roman ships.

events.title: Storm off Pachynus
events.text: A Carthaginian squadron and a storm destroy a second Roman fleet off Sicily's southern cape.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca
events.text: Hamilcar Barca takes command in Sicily and raids the Italian coast from Mount Heirkte.

events.title: Rome's last fleet
events.text: Wealthy Romans fund 200 quinqueremes built on the Rhodian's model.

events.title: Battle of the Aegates
events.text: On 10 March, Lutatius Catulus catches Hanno's laden fleet off the Aegates: 50 Punic ships sink, 70 are taken.

events.title: The Marsala ship
events.text: Around these years, a Punic long ship sinks in shallow water off Isola Lunga, north of Lilybaeum.

events.title: Peace of Lutatius
events.text: Carthage gives up Sicily and the islands between Sicily and Italy, and pays a heavy indemnity.

chartNote: Share of the land area of seven present-day countries, by the navy that controlled each one's coasts and nearby seas. Regions are today's boundaries; Italy stands for Sicily, Sardinia and the mainland together, and the large North African countries swing the shares. Sea control was seasonal and shifting, so this is a simplification.
